q-334626.name: Question 1
q-334626.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $2\pm 3\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
{{field-2}} $\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
q-334626.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 6 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(2+3\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(2-3\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2+3\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2+3\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2+3\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ (2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+{e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
$$

q-334634.name: Question 2
q-334634.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm 3\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}\,\,$ $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ $2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
q-334634.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-3\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3\text{i}t) & ={e}^{3\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot 3\text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+3{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\cdot t+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
$$

q-334729.name: Question 3
q-334729.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$3t$ $1-3t$
q-334729.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(3t)={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1+3t), \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3{e}^{3t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1+3t & -3t \\ 3t & 1-3t\end{aligned}].
$$

q-334733.name: Question 4
q-334733.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $-3t$
{{field-2}} $1-6t$
q-334733.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+6t) \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & =12{e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1+6t & -3t \\ 12t & 1-6t\end{aligned}].
$$
